# Ezekiel 40:1–24 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview: The Interpretive Divide

Before verse-by-verse notes, it is worth noting that Ezekiel 40–48 is one of the most disputed sections of Scripture. Enduring Word (David Guzik, drawing on Taylor, Feinberg, Alexander, and others) lists four major approaches:

1. **Literal-prophetic** – Ezekiel expected the returning exiles to build this temple (e.g., Adam Clarke). Weakness: it was never built.
2. **Symbolic-Christian** – The passage symbolically depicts the Christian church (favoured by early Church Fathers and the Reformers).
3. **Dispensationalist** – Describes a literal future millennial temple, with memorial sacrifices pointing back to the cross.
4. **Apocalyptic/mythic** – Symbolic images drawn from ancient Near Eastern “cosmic mountain” motifs.

Enduring Word adopts the dispensationalist framework, while Gill (Baptist), Ellicott (Anglican), and Ligonier (Reformed) each argue for symbolic/spiritual readings. These differences colour the interpretation of almost every verse.
– https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

---

## v. 1 – The Date of the Vision

**“In the twenty-fifth year of our exile, at the beginning of the year, on the tenth day of the month—in the fourteenth year after Jerusalem had been struck down…”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** This is the final great vision of Ezekiel, about twelve years after the previous dated oracles. The date could be 10 Nisan (religious calendar), the day Israel began preparing the Passover lamb—making it a fitting day to reveal the messianic kingdom. Alternatively, it could be the civil new year (Tishri). The hand of the LORD emphasises divine origin for the minute detail that follows.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran-leaning):** Dates the vision to 575 BC. Argues firmly for Nisan (Abib), the first month per Exodus 12:2, not Tishri. The tenth day was when Passover preparations began—ideal for revealing the new constitution of God’s kingdom. They reject Hitzig’s proposal of a jubilee year.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-40.html

- **Gill (Baptist):** Notes both possibilities: if Tishri, the 10th day was the Day of Atonement (the church receives atonement through Christ); if Nisan, it was the day the Passover lamb was set apart. Adds that the Talmudists considered this a jubilee year.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** Observes that fourteen years after Jerusalem’s fall was sufficient time for judgment to have produced its effect on the exiles’ minds, making it the right moment for brighter hopes. The tenth of Nisan (Passover preparation) is “a most appropriate season for this vision of the Church of the future.”
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/40.htm

---

## v. 2 – The High Mountain and the City-Like Structure

**“In visions of God He took me to the land of Israel and set me on a very high mountain, on whose southern slope was a structure that resembled a city.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The mountain is likely Mount Moriah (so Clarke). The last visionary visit to Jerusalem (Ezek 8–11) showed the temple profaned and God’s glory departing; now Ezekiel sees restoration. The structure “resembled a city” because of its massive walls, courts, and gates (so Trapp).
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** “In the visions of God” is a phrase Ezekiel always applies to symbolic, not literal, representation (cf. Ezek 1–3, 8–11). The “very high mountain” cannot be literal Moriah (surrounded by higher hills) but is a spiritual image (cf. Isa 2:2; Mic 4:1; Rev 21:10). The structure is the greatly enlarged Temple, not a city.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Gill (Baptist):** Since this is visionary and not material, the mountain signifies the strength, visibility, and exalted state of the church of Christ in the latter day (Isa 2:2). The “city” appearance reflects how the church is commonly compared to a city (Ps 87:3).
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** Identifies the mountain as Zion, “exalted above the tops of all the mountains” (Mic 4:1; Isa 2:2; also Ezek 17:22–23). The prophet sees a “city-edifice toward the south,” consistent with approaching from Babylon in the north.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-40.html

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** God communicated the glory of restoration in terms the exiles could understand—the language of Solomon’s glorious age. The vision is metaphorical, not a blueprint.
  – https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-sees-new-temple

---

## v. 3 – The Bronze Man with Measuring Instruments

**“I saw a man whose appearance was like bronze. He was standing in the gateway with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Likely an angelic being, indicated by his radiant (bronze) appearance. Some (Clarke) suggest a personal appearance of Christ or the Angel of the LORD, though not stated. The linen cord was for longer distances, the rod for shorter.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Gill (Baptist):** Identifies the man as “the Messiah, the builder and owner of the city and temple.” Called a “man” because He would become incarnate; His bronze appearance denotes divine glory, purity, strength, and eternal duration. The line and reed signify the sacred Scriptures as the rule and measure of faith and practice. He stands in the gate as Lord and proprietor.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Benson (Methodist-leaning):** The man is “the same no doubt that appeared to the prophet, Ezekiel 1:20… whose name is the Branch, and who builds the temple of the Lord, Zechariah 6:12–13.”
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/ezekiel-40.html

- **Poole:** “Christ who is this man, hath and keeps the reed in his own hand, as the only fit person to take the measures of all.”
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/ezekiel-40.html

- **Pett (evangelical):** A heavenly visitor (cf. Ezek 8:2). The measuring begins at the gate, stressing that “the making available of the people’s access to God” is primarily in view.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-40.html

- **Constable (evangelical/dispensational):** Bronze in Scripture often represents strength (cf. 1 Kgs 4:13; Job 40:18). The man measures as God’s representative.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-40.html

---

## v. 4 – The Charge to See, Hear, and Declare

**“Son of man… look with your eyes, hear with your ears, and pay attention to everything I am going to show you… Report to the house of Israel everything you see.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** Ezekiel must concentrate—“he is not simply a tourist… He is a mediator of divine revelation” (Block). The audience is the house of Israel. This verse introduces four interpretive approaches (see Overview above). Guzik favours the dispensationalist view: a real future millennial temple with memorial sacrifices that look back to Christ, just as the Lord’s Supper is a memorial.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Gill (Baptist):** The title “Son of man” reminds Ezekiel of his frailty and teaches humility. “Set thy heart” means let the mind be engrossed. The charge to declare applies not only to the captives then but to “the church of God in every age.”
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** God was speaking a language the exiles could understand. Ezekiel describes the glory of restoration in terms familiar to his audience. “God’s revelation is progressive”—culminating in Christ.
  – https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-sees-new-temple

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** In his Preliminary Note, argues at length that the vision cannot be literal because: (1) the temple is miles from the city; (2) the precincts are a mile square—larger than ancient Jerusalem; (3) the land division is geographically impossible; (4) animal sacrifices cannot be restored without contradicting Hebrews; (5) no high priest appears; (6) the Day of Atonement is omitted; (7) the life-giving river is physically impossible. Therefore the whole vision is an ideal picture of the Church of the future, given in terms Ezekiel’s contemporaries could grasp.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Pett (evangelical):** The careful attention required indicates this is “no earthly Temple with earthly functions… It is an everlasting heavenly Temple of which the earthly was, and will be, but a shadow.”
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-40.html

---

## v. 5 – The Outer Wall and the Measuring Rod Defined

**“I saw a wall surrounding the temple area. The measuring rod… was six long cubits (each a cubit and a handbreadth)… the wall was one rod thick and one rod high.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The “long cubit” was about 20.5 inches (52 cm), making a rod roughly 10 ft 3 in (3.12 m). The wall was therefore about ten feet thick and high. Measuring signifies claiming ownership: “To measure property is symbolic of claiming it for yourself” (Wiersbe). Ezekiel did not measure—God, through His representative, did.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Ellicott (Anglican):** The “cubit and a handbreadth” is the ancient Mosaic cubit, longer than the common cubit of Ezekiel’s day (cf. 2 Chr 3:3, “cubits after the first measure”). Ezekiel deliberately uses the older sacred standard to distinguish this temple from the post-exilic one.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Gill (Baptist):** The wall serves two purposes: (a) **separation**—between the church and the profane world (Ezek 42:20), grounded in God’s eternal purpose and grace; (b) **protection**—God Himself is the wall, a “wall of fire” (Zech 2:5), securing His people by love, power, and salvation (Isa 26:1).
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Constable (evangelical):** Walls provided a barrier guarding the holiness of God. Measuring implies ownership (cf. Zech 2:1; Rev 11:1; 21:15).
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-40.html

- **Poole:** “The prophet is called to see and hear, but the standard is not put into his hand: Christ… hath and keeps the reed in his own hand.”
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/ezekiel-40.html

---

## vv. 6–10 – The Eastern Gateway: Threshold, Chambers, and Portico

**“Then he came to the gate facing east and climbed its steps. He measured the threshold of the gate to be one rod deep…” through v. 10, describing three gate chambers per side, jambs, and portico.**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The tour begins at the east gate because the glory of God would return through it (Ezek 43). The gate is a tower-like building with compartments (“gate chambers”). These chambers were for priests and Levites to lodge in during their ministration (Poole). The east gate was “in some ways the most important of all” (Feinberg).
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Dummelow:** Provides a precise diagrammatic summary: threshold (a) 6 cubits broad × 10 cubits wide; three guardrooms (b) on each side, each 6 cubits square, separated by wall-spaces of 5 cubits; inner threshold (c) same as outer; porch (d) 8 cubits wide with jambs 2 cubits broad.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-40.html

- **Gill (Baptist):** The east gate represents access to the Gospel church. The chambers are resting-places for ministers and members. The measurements signify the order and proportion of Gospel church discipline.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Pett (evangelical):** The east gate is where the glory returns (Ezek 43). The symmetrical design with three chambers per side represents completeness. The detailed measurements show that in God’s new order everything is perfectly proportioned.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-40.html

---

## vv. 11–16 – East Gate: Entrance Width, Gateposts, Windows, and Palm Trees

Key details: entrance 10 cubits wide, length 13 cubits; chambers 6 cubits square; gate width 25 cubits door-to-door; gateposts 60 cubits high; total length 50 cubits; beveled windows; palm tree decorations.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The gateposts at 60 cubits (about 100 ft / 31.5 m) made the gate a tower-like structure. Beveled windows provided light. Palm trees were “engraven with curious art” for decoration. Guzik notes that “not all the terminology is clear in the Hebrew… the exact meaning of each item… cannot always be certain” (Alexander).
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Dummelow:** The whole gateway length was 50 cubits, breadth 25 cubits. Guardrooms and porch were lit by windows; the wall-spaces between guardrooms also had windows. Palm trees decorated these spaces.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-40.html

- **Taylor (via Enduring Word):** The phrase “as door faces door” (v. 13) suggests a door led from each side room to the outer court, allowing Levitical door-keepers access to control crowds at festival times.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

---

## vv. 17–19 – The Outer Court: Chambers, Pavement, and Measurement to Inner Court

**“Then he brought me into the outer court, and there were chambers and a pavement… Thirty chambers faced the pavement… the lower pavement… distance from the front of the lower gateway to the outside of the inner court… a hundred cubits.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The outer court had thirty chambers, likely for worshippers or storage. The pavement “flanked the gateways” and was called the “lower pavement” because the inner court was on a higher level (cf. v. 31, eight steps up to inner court).
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Gill (Baptist):** The pavement represents the doctrine of the apostles and prophets on which the church is built. The thirty chambers suggest provision for all true Israelites of God in the Gospel church. The 100-cubit distance between outer and inner court indicates “there is a great distance between the outward visible court, or church, and the inward and more spiritual and glorious state of it.”
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Dummelow:** The outer court pavement corresponded to the length of the gates. The “lower pavement” terminology implies the inner court was higher.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/ezekiel-40.html

---

## vv. 20–23 – The North Gate

**“He also measured the length and width of the gateway of the outer court facing north… same measurements as the first gate: fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide… Seven steps led up to it… a gate to the inner court facing the north gate… hundred cubits.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The north gate is an identical reproduction of the east gate in every respect—chambers, pillars, portico, windows, and palm trees. The seven steps (first mentioned here) elevate the temple above ground level.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Pett (evangelical):** The three gates (east, north, south) together represent “complete access.” The seven steps are “the number of divine perfection”—the temple is raised above the earth by a divinely perfect amount and accessed in a divinely perfect way. Seven “often indicated divine activity and perfection” throughout the ancient Near East.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/ezekiel-40.html

- **Gill (Baptist):** The north gate has the same measurements as the east, showing there is “but one way into the Gospel church,” whether Jews or Gentiles enter. The seven steps suggest the perfect and complete work of God’s Spirit in conversion and entrance.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

- **Poole:** The north gate exhibits “exact symmetry” with the east, showing God’s order and harmony.
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/ezekiel-40.html

---

## v. 24 – The South Gate

**“Then he led me to the south side, and I saw a gateway facing south. He measured its side pillars and portico, and they had the same measurements as the others.”**

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** The south gate, like the north, matches the east gate in all measurements. The three gates (east, north, south—no west gate is mentioned in ch. 40) together form the entrances to the outer court. The symmetry underscores the perfection of God’s design.
  – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

- **Poole:** “Having finished the measuring of the east gate, and showed the prophet the sameness of the north gate’s buildings, measures, and ornaments, now he is informed of the south gate, and its exact symmetry with the other two.”
  – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/ezekiel-40.html

- **Gill:** The three gates (east, north, south) all alike show that “the way of admission into the Gospel church is the same” from whatever direction one approaches—by the one door, Christ. Palm trees in all three gates signify joy, victory, and uprightness shared by all true believers.
  – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

---

## Summary of Protestant Traditions on Ezekiel 40:1–24

### Reformed (Ligonier.org)
The vision is **symbolic/metaphorical**. The temple’s dimensions are symbolic (multiples of five; perfect cube unlike Solomon’s). God was communicating in terms the exiles understood—this is not a future building plan. The returning exiles were never condemned for not building Ezekiel’s temple (Hag 1:1–11). Progressive revelation culminates in Christ.
– https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ezekiel-sees-new-temple

### Baptist – Older (Gill)
The entire vision is **mystically/figuratively of the Gospel church**. The man = the Messiah. The wall = God’s love and power separating and protecting the church. The measuring instruments = Scripture as the rule of faith. The gates = Christ as the one door. The palm trees = joy and victory of believers. This temple began to be fulfilled after Christ’s resurrection and will see its ultimate fulfilment in the latter-day glory of the church.
– https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/ezekiel/40.htm

### Baptist/Reformed – Modern (DesiringGod / GTY)
Searches did not return specific verse-by-verse content from desiringgod.org or gty.org for this passage within the search limits. No distinct Baptist position beyond Gill’s symbolic reading could be verified from these sources.

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word – David Guzik)
Adopts the **dispensationalist framework**: the temple is a real, literal structure to be built during a future millennial reign of Christ. Animal sacrifices will be **memorials** looking back to the cross, not atoning in themselves—parallel to the Lord’s Supper as a memorial. Key missing elements (no high priest, no ark, no veil, no Pentecost) argue for a post-cross setting.
– https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-40/

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Strongly argues for a **purely ideal/symbolic** reading. The Preliminary Note lists extensive reasons why literal fulfilment is impossible: geographical impossibilities, contradictions with the New Testament (Hebrews, Galatians), omission of the Day of Atonement and high priest, changes to Mosaic law, and the physically impossible river. The vision is an ideal picture of the Church of the future, clothed in terms the exiles would understand.
– https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/ezekiel/40.htm

### Lutheran (Keil & Delitzsch)
While Keil & Delitzsch do not adopt a purely symbolic approach, they treat the vision as a **prophetic vision of a real future restoration**, grounded in the literal site of Zion. They take the measurements seriously as describing an actual structure, though the full excerpt was not available for vv. 6–24.
– https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/ezekiel-40.html

### Evangelical/Dispensationalist (Constable, Gray)
**Gray’s Concise Commentary**: “These chapters give a picture of the restored temple at Jerusalem during the Millennium, and of the worship of the Messiah when He shall exercise sway from that center to the ends of the earth.”
– https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jgc/ezekiel-40.html

**Constable**: The vision describes a millennial temple. Measuring implies divine ownership. The detail distinguishes this temple from any past structure.
– https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-40.html
